groups.instructions: Read the passage about the school weather postcard exchange and choose the best answer.
groups.passage:
Two secondary schools, one in the highland village of Birch Pass and the other on the island of Sunhaven, began a weather postcard project in September. Teachers wanted students to compare everyday life in places with different landscapes. Each class kept a simple diary of temperature, clouds and rainfall, then wrote a postcard every Friday describing one surprising observation.

At first, several island students assumed that the highland village was covered in snow for most of the year. Some highland students imagined the island was always sunny. The September diaries challenged both ideas. Birch Pass had mild afternoons but chilly mornings, while Sunhaven experienced strong winds and a week of heavy showers.

Because postal deliveries to the island were sometimes delayed by rough seas, the schools agreed to exchange photographs of the cards through a private classroom platform as well. Teachers obtained parental permission before any photographs showing students were shared. The handwritten cards still arrived later and were displayed in both schools.

During an online meeting, pupils compared records from the same dates and noticed that one place could be cool and dry while the other was warm and wet. Their teachers reminded them that a few weeks of classroom observations could not replace official climate records or weather forecasts. At the end of term, families visited an exhibition of cards, drawings and temperature charts. Students said the project taught them to question assumptions, check dates and listen carefully to people whose daily routines were different from their own.

questions.question_text: What was the project's main purpose?

options.text: To identify the best place for a new airport.
To predict next year's exact rainfall.
To compare daily weather and life in two different places.

questions.question_text: What did some island students originally believe about Birch Pass?

options.text: It was snowy during most of the year.
It was located beside a warm sea.

questions.question_text: Which information did the classes record in their diaries?

options.text: The price of food on the island.

questions.question_text: Why were photographs of postcards exchanged online?

options.text: Teachers wanted to cancel handwriting lessons.
Students had lost all the original cards.
Postal deliveries to the island were sometimes delayed.
The online meeting was the only school activity.

questions.question_text: What did teachers do before sharing photographs that showed students?

options.text: They asked the town council to buy cameras.
They published the photographs in a newspaper.
They waited until the exhibition ended.

questions.question_text: What did the pupils discover when comparing the same dates?

options.text: Weather conditions could differ greatly between the two places.
The two schools always had identical weather.
Temperature changes were caused by the postcards.

questions.question_text: The word 'assumptions' in the final paragraph is closest in meaning to -------.
Why did the teachers caution against relying only on the diaries?

options.text: They believed students could not write accurately.
The postcards were printed on thin paper.
A few weeks of observations were insufficient for official climate conclusions.

questions.question_text: Who attended the end-of-term exhibition?

options.text: People who had never visited a school.

questions.question_text: Which lesson did students say they had learned?

options.text: To test their expectations against evidence and listen to others.
To trust their first guesses about other places.
To stop comparing dates in weather records.
To replace local forecasts with postcards.

groups.instructions: Read the passage about waste-heat recovery at a swimming pool and answer the questions.
groups.passage:
Heated water is essential for Millcross's indoor swimming pool, yet rising energy bills had forced the town council to consider shortening opening hours. A young engineer noticed that a small data centre next door released a steady stream of heat as its computers operated. She proposed using some of that otherwise wasted heat to warm the pool.

The design used a heat exchanger, a device that transfers heat between two separate water systems. Warm water from the data centre passed through one side of the exchanger, while pool water moved through the other. The two supplies never mixed. A conventional heater remained available for especially cold days or unexpected breakdowns.

During a three-month trial, technicians measured water temperature, electricity use and maintenance time. Early reports appeared to show enormous savings. However, the pool had been closed for five days during the first month to repair damaged tiles. Those closed days required much less energy, so comparing the total monthly bills gave a misleading picture. The team corrected the calculation by comparing days with similar opening hours and temperatures.

The revised results showed moderate savings, although maintenance costs were higher than expected. Residents also wanted assurance that extra pumps would not create noise at night. The engineer proposed sound insulation and a maintenance schedule. Before paying for a larger system, the council requested an independent energy audit. It hoped the project would show that useful innovations could be assessed carefully before public money was committed.

questions.question_text: What is the main subject of the passage?

options.text: A plan to replace an indoor pool with a data centre.
A competition to design swimming equipment.
A trial that used a data centre's surplus heat to warm a pool.
A course teaching computers to monitor swimmers.

questions.question_text: Why was the council considering shorter pool opening hours?

options.text: The pool had no clean water.

questions.question_text: How did the heat exchanger keep the two water supplies separate?

options.text: It sent both supplies to the same open tank.
It replaced all pool water with data-centre water.

It transferred heat between separate circuits without mixing the water.

questions.question_text: Which measurements were collected during the trial?

options.text: Water temperature, electricity use and maintenance time.

The number of computers sold by the data centre.

questions.question_text: Why did the first savings estimate appear too high?

options.text: The technicians had measured the air rather than the water.
The data centre had stopped working for three months.
The town council had invented the electricity bills.
The pool had been closed for repairs on five days, reducing energy demand.

questions.question_text: In the passage, 'moderate savings' most nearly means -------.

options.text: a complete removal of all costs
a noticeable but limited reduction in costs

options.text: The pool might change its name.

options.text: A larger room for the data-centre computers.

options.text: All engineering projects should be accepted immediately.
